newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG's Chan "in aboslute control", army chief defiant.
newsitem.headline: PNG's Chan "in aboslute control", army chief defiant.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said on Tuesday his government was in "absolute control" of the South Pacific nation after the sacking of its rebellious army chief.
"The government is in absolute control of the situation," Chan told a news conference. "The institution of democracy is very much alive...in this country."
Chan described Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok's demand on Monday that he and other ministers resign within 48 hours as "gross insubordination and bordering on treason".
And he said Singirok was being investigated by police after what Chan himself considered an attempted coup.

Singirok brought about one of the worst crises in Papua New Guinea's 22 years of independence when he gave Chan an ultimatum to quit over his decision to use mercenaries against an island rebellion on Bougainville.
Singirok urged restraint on his own troops during the crisis and consistently denied he was mounting a coup against Chan.
Chan said the new acting defence force chief, Colonel Alfred Aikung, had reported that all army and police units were in complete support of the government.
"All the disciplinary members (army and police) of this country have pledged their support to the government of this country," Chan said.
He said 40 foreign mercenaries, detained by Singirok on Monday, would be released later on Tuesday and their operation against the nine-year-old Bougainville uprising would go ahead as planned.
Singirok remained defiant, saying after accepting his formal dismissal notice that his campaign against Chan would continue.
"The issue of Sandline (a British-based mercenary outfit) is not closed, as what this government is doing I believe is wrong," Singirok said in a statement.
"It has mortgaged the country to foreigners at the expense of our four million Papua New Guineans."

Singirok had said Chan would be removed from office if he refused to go, but Tuesday's statement seemed to signal that the army chief -- said to be popular with his troops -- was now embarking on a political campaign.

The streets of Port Moresby were calm but tense as the army and police force waited for the standoff to be resolved. The only rumblings to be heard were from intermittent tropical rainstorms over the city.

Singirok, a 40-year-old career soldier trained in Australia, turned against Chan for his decision to contract Sandline International to help end the conflict on resource-rich Bougainville, 800 kms (500 miles) northeast of the capital.
Sandline in turn hired mercenaries from the South African-based private army Executive Outcomes.
Monday's uncertainty sent the shares of major investors in the country downwards, although PNG stocks listed on the Australian stock exchange began to recover ground on Tuesday.
Australia, a close neighbour and the nation's biggest aid donor, on Tuesday backed Chan's decision to sack Singirok, though Canberra has opposed the use of mercenaries.

"We utterly deplore the attempts of (the) former commander-in-chief of the Papua New Guinea defence force to defy the authority of the duly elected government of Papua New Guinea," Australian Prime Minister John Howard said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
